questions.question: When the tide goes out, it leaves a small pool of seawater among the rocks of a shore. Snails, crabs, seaweed and tiny fish live in the pool, with the water, the rocks and the sunlight all around them. What is the name for all of these together, the living and the nonliving, acting on one another?
choices: An ecosystem
A community
A population
A food web
questions.context: A tide pool is a tiny but complete ecosystem: its living things together with the water, rocks, air and sunlight around them, each acting on the others. A community is only the living things, a population is the members of one kind, and a food web shows only who eats whom.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.12A has 5th graders describe how organisms in an ecosystem interact with its living and nonliving parts, which starts from what an ecosystem is.

questions.question: In a mountain valley, pine trees cover the slopes, deer graze in the meadow and bacteria live in the soil. What do ecologists call the living parts of an ecosystem, such as these?
choices: Biotic factors
Abiotic factors
Habitats
Producers
questions.context: The living parts of an ecosystem, its plants, animals, fungi and bacteria, are its biotic factors; the nonliving parts, such as sunlight, water, air, soil and rock, are its abiotic factors. Producers are only the living things that make their own food, like the pine trees, and a habitat is the place where a living thing makes its home.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.12A names biotic and abiotic factors, so 5th graders learn the word for the living parts of an ecosystem.

questions.question: Ecologists call the nonliving parts of an ecosystem its abiotic factors. Around a pond, each of these animals is making use of something near it. Which one is using an abiotic factor?
questions.answer: A turtle warming up on a sunny rock
choices: A turtle warming up on a sunny rock
A frog catching a passing fly
A duck nibbling the pondweed's leaves
A fish hiding in a thick bed of weeds
questions.context: Sunlight and rock are both nonliving, and turtles, like lizards, warm their bodies by basking in the sun, for they take their body heat from their surroundings. The frog, the duck and the fish are each using another living thing: an insect to eat, a plant to eat, and plants to hide among.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.12A asks 5th graders how organisms survive by interacting with abiotic factors such as sunlight, rock and temperature.

questions.question: A forest gives the animals that live in it food to eat, streams to drink from, places to hide and rest, and room enough to roam. What is the forest to each of these animals?
choices: Its habitat
Its shelter
Its niche
Its food web
questions.context: A habitat is the place where a living thing makes its home and finds all it needs: food, water, shelter and space. A den is only shelter, one part of a habitat; a niche is the job a living thing does in its ecosystem; and a food web is only the pattern of who eats whom.
questions.grade_note: Habitat as the place that gives a living thing its food, water, shelter and space is basic 5th-grade ecosystem vocabulary.

questions.question: Ecologists judge an ecosystem's health in several ways, such as how clean its water is and how well it stands up to trouble. Which kind of ecosystem usually stands up best to a drought or a disease?
questions.answer: One with many kinds of living things
choices: One with many kinds of living things
One with many animals of only a few kinds
One with only the strongest kinds
One with no predators at all
questions.context: Many different kinds of living things, called biodiversity, usually make an ecosystem stronger: when a disease killed most of the chestnut trees in some great forests, the forests lived on because other kinds of trees grew there too. Predators belong in a healthy ecosystem as well, and taking them away can throw a whole food web out of balance.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.12C asks 5th graders to describe a healthy ecosystem, and many different kinds of living things is the first mark of one that they are taught.

questions.question: Workers cut every tree from a steep hillside and clear the ground bare to make way for new houses. In the next heavy rains, much of the hill's soil washes down into the valley below. Why does the soil wash away so easily now?
questions.answer: No roots hold the soil together
choices: No roots hold the soil together
The soil has lost its nutrients
The soil is lighter without the trees
Rain soaks into bare ground faster
questions.context: Tree roots grip the soil and bind it together, and without them heavy rain carries it off and muddies the streams below. Taking the trees away does not change the soil's own weight, and bare ground soaks up less rain than ground full of roots, so more water runs over the top.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.12C names cutting down forests among the human activities that harm an ecosystem, and soil washing off the bare land is the plainest result.

questions.question: Rain washes fertilizer from farm fields into a lake. Algae grow so thickly that the water turns green, and when the algae die and rot, many of the lake's fish die too. What kills the fish?
questions.answer: Too little oxygen in the water
choices: Too little oxygen in the water
Too little light in the water
Too much heat in the water
Too little food in the water
questions.context: The fertilizer feeds the algae, and when they die, bacteria break them down and use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Fish breathe that oxygen, so when it runs low they suffocate; the darker, greener water is not what kills them.
questions.grade_note: Mystery Science's grade 5 ecosystems unit (NGSS 5-ESS3-1) teaches how fertilizer runoff makes algae blooms that harm a lake's fish.

questions.question: A town wants to help the fish, frogs and birds that live in its lake, and its people put forward four plans. Which plan helps them?
questions.answer: Planting shrubs and tall grasses along the shore
choices: Planting shrubs and tall grasses along the shore
Mowing the lawn right down to the water's edge
Pulling the fallen logs out of the water
Feeding bread to the ducks every day
questions.context: A strip of wild plants along the shore catches soil and fertilizer before rain can wash them into the lake, and its deep roots hold the bank, while a lawn's roots reach down only a few centimetres. Fallen logs give fish shelter and places to feed, and soggy leftover bread rots in the water and feeds the algae.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.12C asks 5th graders how human activities help or harm an ecosystem, and restoring the plants along a shore is one of the helpful ones.

463a176a36.why: Judge (medium): the stem defined 'biotic' as 'living', so sorting moss from wind gave the term away, and 'The moss' repeated food-chains-and-food-webs' producer key with the same reasoning. The question now tests the term itself (F2): living examples with no moss, keyed 'Biotic factors' against 'Abiotic factors', 'Habitats' and 'Producers' (the pine trees are producers, the deer and the bacteria are not).

b91ab91c11.why: Judge (medium): nectar is a nonliving liquid, so 'A bee sipping nectar' was a second defensible answer; judge (low) and lead: the desert lizard with a hawk repeated adaptations-built-for-a-place's camouflage scene. The scene moves to a pond: a basking turtle (F29) against a frog eating a fly, a duck eating pondweed and a fish sheltering in water plants, where the thing used is plainly alive (F30, F31). No lizard or hawk remains in this unit.

1ff52c5397.why: Judge (medium, lane): the stem was built on the mountain lion's own natural history (F12), the animal bank's. It now speaks of a forest's animals in general (F11), with the same key. Judge (low): 'Its climate' was a dead lure; 'Its food web' replaces it (a forest has a food web but is not one, F5).

bb08c5a01e.why: Fact-check (error): the context said no single animal can change its body to need less water, but some frogs aestivate, slowing their bodies in the mud through a drought (F32). It now says no animal grows a new kind of body, and that such frogs were born able to wait. Judge (medium): the key was the only hedged choice; every choice now opens with 'Some', and the Lamarck lure says 'grow new bodies', which is wrong even for aestivating frogs (F17, F32). Stem and key unchanged.

f6925c3f76.why: Judge (medium): 'trees, stumps and all' pointed at the roots, and 'The soil turns to sand without shade' was no real misconception. The stem now says only that the ground is cleared bare, and 'The soil is lighter without the trees' (a child's idea that heavy trees press the soil down, F33) replaces the sand choice. Key unchanged.

dropped.question: Year after year, little rain falls on a marsh, until its pools dry up and its mud bakes hard. What usually happens to the living things there?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: The judge's tell is only moved, not fixed. Every choice now opens with 'Some', but each wrong choice still makes an absolute claim in its second clause ('the rest grow new bodies', 'no new kinds ever move in', 'the plants are unharmed'), so the key is still the only choice with no absolute. Also, 'the plants are unharmed' falls to the stem's own dried pools and baked mud, so only the key and the Lamarck lure are live. The judge's fix (take the absolutes out of the wrong choices) was not applied. The facts are sound: the context's aestivation line is now true.
